verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to YHWH, call on his name, make known among the peoples his deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks to the LORD. Call out his name aloud, and carry word of what he has done to the peoples, out to the far edges of the nations.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a call to a crowd. Three imperatives in a row, each a plural command, and every actor on stage must feel that he is addressing a congregation, not himself. Radak and Meiri say this psalm's opening is the song David handed to Asaph to sing before the ark (1 Chr 16:8-22); even without that setting, the tone is that of a liturgy being led.

The KJV has "call upon his name" and "the people". The Hebrew has the preposition bet, 'in/by his name', so the calling is done with the name on the lips. Metzudat David reads 'his name' as the name that belongs to him alone. The KJV also puts "the people" in the singular, though the Hebrew has the plural 'amim: the nations, and not Israel. The third command therefore takes the praise outside the community. 'Alilot, "deeds", is not neutral either: the word often means a doing that is bold or strikingly deliberate, and Rashi glosses it with ma'alalav, 'his doings'. It is a recital of what he has done, not an abstract thanks.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of yadah. It means 'give thanks' and also 'acknowledge publicly, confess'. The thanks is a spoken act, not a feeling, and a near-identical sound, hodu from yadah, sets up the call to 'make known' (hodi'u, from yada') in the same verse. The two roots are different; the echo is of sound only.
'Deeds' in the sense of things done to or against someone; Rashi glosses it as ma'alalav. The next verses fill it with wonders, signs and judgments against Egypt.

verses.translation_literal: Sing to him, make music to him, muse on all his wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing to him. Let strings and voices rise to him. And when the singing stops, do not let the talk turn to small things: speak of his wonders, all of them.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three verbs for three ways of making sound. Shiru is singing with the voice, zamru is music with an instrument (Ibn Ezra: with the voice and with the lyre; Metzudat David: by mouth and by instrument). Siḥu is the odd one out: it is talk, the half-murmured speech of a man going over something in his mind, and the same verb is used of someone complaining or musing. The KJV's "talk ye" is fair; the BBE's "let all your thoughts be" drifts toward silent thought, and the Hebrew says it is spoken.

Meiri hears an ethic in it: even in ordinary conversation, nothing idle, only his wonders. Stage it as the move from the sung line to the spoken one, from the platform to the table.

philological_notes.note: To muse aloud, to speak at length about something. The verb sits between speech and meditation, which is why the English versions split between 'talk', 'meditate' and 'thoughts'.

verses.translation_literal: Boast in the name of his holiness; let the heart of those who seek YHWH rejoice.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take pride in his holy name, and wear it as your own glory. Let the heart rejoice in every one who goes looking for the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Boast' is a sharp word here. The Hithpael of halal is the verb from which 'hallelujah' comes, but the reflexive stem makes it 'make yourselves praised': you are to feel pride in your God the way a client feels it in his patron. Rashi says exactly this, that you have a patron like no one else's. The KJV's "glory ye in" is archaic but accurate; the BBE's "have glory in" loses the self-regarding edge.

'The name of his holiness' is a construct chain, not an adjective, so the KJV's "his holy name" makes the holiness an attribute. The Hebrew has the name as something that belongs to the holiness itself.

The second half moves from the loud to the quiet. The seekers' hearts are not told to shout, only to be glad. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'seekers' as possibly including the nations who do not yet know the name.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of halal: 'boast, take credit and pride in'. It is used where the praise falls back on the praiser, and here the praise is of Israel's own possession, a patron nobody else has.
'Those who seek YHWH': a participle, so it is a habit and an identity, not a single act. The next verse turns the same root into an imperative.

verses.translation_literal: Seek YHWH and his strength; seek his face continually.
verses.translation_dramatic: Seek the LORD, and seek his strength. Seek his face. Seek it without pause, and do not stop.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two different verbs for 'seek', darash and baqqesh, and the second is the intensive (Piel) stem. The seeking is more than looking: darash is the verb for going to inquire, to consult a deity or an oracle, and the actors should play it as going to ask for help. 'His face' is the idiom for his presence: to seek the face is to ask for an audience.

The KJV's "evermore" is correct for tamid, but the word is the one used of the 'continual' offering, the daily service, and so the verse has a liturgical rhythm, not only a mood. What 'his strength' means is disputed. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'uz as the ark (as in Ps 78:61, 'he gave his strength into captivity'), which fits the setting they assume for the psalm; Meiri reads it as the strength he shows in battle. The plain reading is the strength of God himself.

philological_notes.note: 'His strength', which Ibn Ezra and Radak take as a name for the ark of the covenant; I treat that as one reading, and the plain sense is God's own might.
'Continually', also the term for the daily 'continual' offering. The word carries the weight of a regular rite as well as of an attitude.

verses.translation_literal: Remember his wonders which he did, his signs and the judgments of his mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember what he did. Remember the wonders, the signs, and the sentences that came out of his own mouth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first of three memory commands; it opens the psalm's long recital. The hymn leaves the call to praise and starts to list evidence. Three things are remembered, and the three words are not synonyms: niflaot are wonders, mofetim are signs or portents that point to something beyond themselves, and mishpetim are verdicts. The KJV's "his marvellous works ... his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth" renders niflaot and mofetim with two different English words, and so keeps them distinct, as the Hebrew does.

'Judgments of his mouth' is the line to play carefully. Radak and Malbim say these were the plagues on Egypt, announced in advance by word before they fell (so the judgment was pronounced in speech before it was carried out). Ibn Ezra puts the wonders in creation, the signs in Egypt and the judgments at Sinai; the verse itself does not assign them.

philological_notes.note: 'Signs, portents': marvellous acts that serve as proof. In the Exodus tradition the word is paired with 'signs' ('otot) as the evidence of divine power. Ibn Ezra assigns it to Egypt.
'The judgments of his mouth': verdicts that he spoke before they happened. Radak ties it to the plagues, announced through Moses before they fell.

verses.translation_literal: Seed of Abraham his servant, sons of Jacob his chosen ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, the seed of Abraham, his servant. You, the sons of Jacob, the ones he chose.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the addressee is named for the first time, and the second-person plural of the earlier commands finally has a face. The line is a vocative with no verb: the speaker turns to the audience and says who they are. In the KJV's "O ye" the vocative is right, but "his chosen" is a singular collective, while the Hebrew has the plural bechirav, 'his chosen ones'; Jacob's sons are chosen one by one, and not as a mass.

Two patriarchs are named, and the order matters. Abraham is 'servant' ('eved), a word of status as well as of work: a servant of the king is a trusted office-holder, not a slave. Jacob's sons are the chosen. Ibn Ezra says Abraham is named as the first to receive the commands, and Jacob as the single father of the nation; Radak says 'seed of Abraham' means Israel only, not all of Abraham's descendants. The parallel in 1 Chr 16:13 has 'seed of Israel his servant', which Radak mentions as saying the same.

philological_notes.note: 'His servant': a title of honour, used of Abraham, Moses, David and the prophets. The title marks a relation of trust and service to a master, and does not mark the status of a slave.
'His chosen ones', a plural. Radak distinguishes the sons of Jacob, chosen, from the rest of Abraham's descendants.

verses.translation_literal: He, YHWH, our God; in all the earth his judgments.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the LORD, our God. And his judgments are not shut inside our borders: they fall across the whole earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbless clauses, so the verse has the clipped, creedal sound of a confession: 'He, YHWH, our God' and then 'in all the earth, his judgments'. The KJV adds "is" and "are" and makes them flowing sentences; the Hebrew has only the bare statements, and a speaker should place the weight on 'our'.

The tension is between the particular and the universal. He is 'our God', the one with a covenant, and yet his judgments are in all the earth. Radak puts it directly: although his rule covers the world, he is our God and we are his people. Malbim says the suffix 'our' shows the special bond. The BBE's "he is judge of all the earth" turns the second clause into a title, and loses the plural, mishpatav, a set of particular verdicts.

philological_notes.note: 'His judgments': in the plural, the individual rulings and acts of government, so not one abstract justice. The same word closed v. 5 as 'judgments of his mouth'.

verses.translation_literal: He remembers for ever his covenant, the word he commanded, for a thousand generations.
verses.translation_dramatic: He remembers. He has always remembered his covenant, the word he laid down, and he will remember it a thousand generations on.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar here is worth the actors' attention: zakhar is a perfect verb ('he has remembered / he remembers'), which in a psalm of praise is a timeless statement, so the KJV's "hath remembered" gives it too much of a one-time past. The command of v. 5 was 'remember', and now God is the one who remembers. 'Remember' in Hebrew is not a memory, it is acting on what you remember; Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'that he not forget'.

'A thousand generations' is a round number that means 'without limit': Meiri says it is not exact but means a long time, and Metzudat David links it to Deut 7:9, 'who keeps covenant and kindness to those who love him, to a thousand generations'. Rashi gives a bolder reading, that the 'word' is the Torah and that God took 974 generations out of the thousand; that is his reading and not what the text states. 'The word he commanded' sits in apposition to the covenant, and the KJV keeps that.

philological_notes.note: 'Remember', as an act and not a thought: to act on a commitment. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'that he not forget'.
'To a thousand generations': a number for the unbounded. It echoes Deut 7:9 in Metzudat David's reading. Rashi has a second reading, 974 generations before the Torah.

verses.translation_literal: Which he cut with Abraham, and his oath to Isaac.
verses.translation_dramatic: The covenant he cut with Abraham, and the oath he swore to Isaac.
verses.directors_commentary:
The covenant is 'cut', karat. The KJV's "made" smooths over what the Hebrew keeps as a physical image: in the ancient Near East a covenant was sealed by cutting animals in two and walking between the pieces, which is the scene at Genesis 15, 'on that day YHWH cut a covenant with Abram'. Meiri and Rashi both point to Gen 15 for this verse. The audience would hear the knife in the verb.

The second half moves from covenant to oath. Radak ties the oath to the binding of Isaac (Gen 22:16-18), and Ibn Ezra to Gen 26:3, where God tells Isaac 'I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father'. The KJV treats this as a single object in two halves, "covenant... and his oath". The Hebrew gives a second noun, shevu'ato, and the second noun is the 'oath' proper.

Meiri notes the spelling Yishchaq with sin instead of the more common Yitzchaq, as Metzudat Zion glosses 'like Yitzchaq'. The spelling is unusual, and nothing in the verse turns on it.

philological_notes.note: 'He cut': the standard verb for making a covenant, literally 'to cut'. It recalls the rite at Genesis 15, where animals were divided and the parties passed between the parts.
'To Isaac', spelled with sin. Metzudat Zion says it is the same as the ordinary spelling with tsade, and Meiri notes the oddity.

verses.translation_literal: And he stood it up for Jacob as a statute, for Israel a covenant of perpetuity.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he set it firm for Jacob as a law that cannot be moved, and for Israel as a covenant that has no end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is vaya'amideha, 'he made it stand', the causative of 'amad: God sets the covenant upright like a post. The KJV's "confirmed the same" is acceptable but pale. What it stands as is a choq, a statute, something carved or fixed. The KJV has "a law", the ASV "a statute", and the second is nearer to the Hebrew: a choq is a fixed boundary, an engraved decree, and not a body of legislation.

The passage runs down the three patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and then Jacob and 'Israel'. The two names are one man in the narrative, but here they stand in parallel: Jacob for a statute, Israel for a covenant of perpetuity. Radak says the point is that the covenant fell on the chosen line only and not on Esau; Meiri says it is a doubling for emphasis, and Malbim, on the contrary, finds a rising scale in the two names. Staged simply, the two halves are one gesture repeated for effect.

philological_notes.note: 'As a statute': from the root meaning to cut or engrave, so a fixed, written ordinance. Metzudat David glosses it 'a fixed law'.
'A covenant of perpetuity': 'olam is time without a visible horizon, and so 'ever', 'perpetual'. Meiri notes that the pairing repeats the 'for ever' of v. 8.

verses.translation_literal: Saying, To you I will give the land of Canaan, the measured portion of your inheritance.
verses.translation_dramatic: And these were the words: "To you I will give the land of Canaan, the plot that will be your own."
verses.directors_commentary:
At last the covenant has content, and it is real estate. The covenant words are quoted directly: 'to you I give the land of Canaan'. 'To you' is singular, because it was said to each patriarch in turn, as Radak and Meiri say; 'your inheritance' is plural, 'your' in the sense of all of you. The shift is in the Hebrew, and the speaker should let the address widen on the last word.

The key noun is chevel, which is literally a rope or measuring line: land was surveyed and allotted with a cord, so 'the portion of your inheritance' is 'the line-measured share'. The KJV's "the lot" gives the sense of allotment, drawn from the casting of lots, which is a different picture; the BBE's "measured line" is nearer to the root. Metzudat Zion cites Joshua 19 for chevel as a district and a share. The ancient audience would hear the surveyor's cord.

A piece of ancient law lies behind it: nachalah is hereditary land that passes down a family, which cannot be sold out of it for good. Calling Canaan a nachalah says the gift is permanent and tied to the family.

philological_notes.note: Literally a rope or cord, used for measuring out land and so for 'a measured portion, an allotment'. Metzudat Zion cites Joshua 19 for the sense of district and share.
Hereditary holding, land that passes within a family. It implies permanence and entitlement, and so the gift is not a lease.

verses.translation_literal: When they were men of number, like a little, and sojourners in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: They were so few then, men you could count on your fingers, hardly anyone at all, and strangers in a land that was not yet theirs.
verses.directors_commentary:
The promise of the last verse is set against its moment, and the contrast is the point. 'Men of number' (metei mispar) is an idiom for 'a countable few': the group is small enough to be reckoned one by one (compare Gen 34:30 and Deut 4:27). The KJV's "but a few men in number" gets the sense, and then adds "yea, very few" for kim'at, which is literally 'like a little': hardly anything, a handful.

The last word is the sting. Gerim are resident aliens, people with no land of their own and no rights beyond the host's tolerance: no inheritance, no family plot, no legal standing. The one who owns the whole land by promise lives in it as a guest. Radak adds that the patriarchs even had to leave it, to Egypt and to Philistia, in famine. Malbim reads the two phrases as small in number and 'almost' small in strength, and the point is that the promise was made to a people who looked nothing like a nation. The ASV and KJV agree on "sojourners/strangers"; 'sojourners' is better for the legal sense.

philological_notes.note: 'Men of number': an idiom for so few that they can be counted. The noun mat, 'man', occurs only in the plural (construct metei), and almost only in fixed phrases like this one.
'Sojourners', resident aliens without land or full legal standing. The word marks the patriarchs' status in Canaan, as guests in a land promised to them.

verses.translation_literal: And they went about from nation to nation, from a kingdom to another people.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they walked on, a family with no fixed address, from one nation's border to the next, out of one kingdom and into the lands of strangers.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb is a Hithpael, וַיִּתְהַלְּכוּ: not 'went' once but 'kept walking to and fro, went about'. This is the restless gait of herders on someone else's ground. Play it as a movement with no destination: tents folded, flocks driven, always a guest. The KJV's 'When they went' links the clause to the previous verse as a simple time marker and flattens the continuous action; the ASV 'went about' is closer. The two pairs of nouns are not mere repetition: goy ('nation') and mamlakhah ('kingdom') step up from a people to an organised state with a king, which prepares verse 14, where kings enter the scene. Malbim reads the sequence the same way, as a rise from peoples to kings.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of halakh: repeated, habitual or aimless walking, 'to walk about, to roam'. It is the verb used of God walking in the garden (Gen 3:8) and of Enoch walking with God, so the sense is a lifestyle, not a single journey. KJV 'went' loses the iterative force.
Rashi (Gen 21:34; 12:10; 26; 42) reads the clause as the patriarchs' sojourns among Philistines, Egypt and Canaan; Metzudat David adds that a lone foreigner had no protection, which sets up verse 14.

verses.translation_literal: He did not let a man oppress them, and he rebuked kings on their account.
verses.translation_dramatic: No hand was allowed to press down on them. No one dared. And when kings reached for what was theirs, it was the LORD who spoke against the kings, for their sake.
verses.directors_commentary: A migrant family with no citizenship, no land and no army was legally prey in the ancient Near East: the stranger could be robbed, enslaved or taken into a harem, and no one would answer for it. Metzudat David notes exactly this custom. The verse answers it: God stands in for the missing protector. Speak the first half quietly, as a fact of protection, and the second with weight: the rebuke is aimed upward at kings, not at ordinary oppressors. The KJV 'suffered no man to do them wrong' is archaic ('suffer' meaning allow); the Hebrew hinniach is 'let rest, left alone, permitted'. 'Do them wrong' also softens אָשַׁק, which is 'defraud, extort, oppress by force'. The BBE 'kept back kings' mistranslates the Hiphil of יכח, 'to rebuke, set right, reprove'. The commentators fill in the examples from Genesis (Pharaoh struck with plagues, Gen 12:17; Abimelech's household closed up, Gen 20:18), but the psalm leaves the kings unnamed so that the pattern, not the incident, carries the claim.

philological_notes.note: Oppress, extort, exploit by power. It is the verb of economic and physical abuse of the weak (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14), stronger than KJV 'do wrong'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as oppression and robbery.
Hiphil of yakhach: to reprove, decide against, bring a case. Here God acts as judge: Rashi gives the plague on Pharaoh and the closing of Abimelech's household as the rebuke.

verses.translation_literal: Do not touch my anointed ones, and to my prophets do not do evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Do not lay a hand on my anointed. Do no harm to my prophets."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the one line of direct speech in the stretch, and it is God speaking to kings: a warning in his own voice, a short, hard command with two prohibitions that mirror each other. Say it flat, almost cold, like a notice on a border post. Verse 14 told us that God rebuked kings; here we hear what he said. The word 'anointed' (mashiach) is plural, 'my anointed ones', and does not yet mean the Messiah. It is the Hebrew word for someone set apart, and the commentators read it as the patriarchs themselves, honoured like kings without a crown (Radak, Meiri; Rashi: 'my great ones'). In Genesis, Abraham is called a 'prince of God' (Gen 23:6) and a prophet (Gen 20:7), which is what draws the two titles together. The KJV 'Touch not mine anointed' is accurate but it silently turns a plural into a singular and gives modern readers a reason to hear 'the Messiah'; the ASV's 'anointed ones' keeps the plural. The BBE's 'marked with my holy oil' explains the image but adds the oil, which the verse does not mention. 'Touch' (nagaʿ) is a mild-sounding verb that also means 'strike' or 'afflict' (Gen 12:17, where God 'touched' Pharaoh with plagues), so the line threatens as well as forbids.

philological_notes.note: Plural with a first-person suffix: 'my anointed ones'. In the patriarchal stories nobody is anointed with oil; the word is a title of status, as Rashi says ('my great ones') and Radak ('princes and great men'). The sense 'the Messiah' is a later development.
'Touch', but also 'strike, afflict'; the noun nega' is a 'plague'. Metzudat David reads the plagues of Pharaoh as the 'touch' that God returned.

verses.translation_literal: And he called a famine upon the land; every staff of bread he broke.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then he called for hunger, and hunger came. It fell on the land, and every staff that bread leans on, he snapped.
verses.directors_commentary: Two images carry the verse. First, God 'calls' the famine like a servant summoned; Ibn Ezra and Radak say the idiom shows that every decree of God is carried by a word. Elisha's line, 'the LORD has called for a famine' (2 Kings 8:1), uses the same words (Meiri cites it). The KJV 'called for' is fine; the BBE 'took away all food' loses the personification. Second, 'staff of bread' (mateh lechem) is a vivid phrase that the translators often clear away. Bread is the walking stick of a poor household: the thing that holds the body up. To 'break the staff' is to leave people leaning on nothing (cf. Lev 26:26, Ezek 4:16). The KJV's 'brake the whole staff of bread' keeps the image but in outdated spelling. In Canaan, a famine means failed winter rains and failed barley, and the grain stores of a small household last about a year at most. Play this at the moment when the sky has been empty too long.

philological_notes.note: 'Staff of bread', i.e. the support on which life leans. Radak glosses it as mish'an lechem, 'support of bread'; Metzudat Zion says the word 'staff' is borrowed from leaning on a stick.
God 'calls' the famine, as in 2 Kings 8:1. Both Ibn Ezra and Meiri take it as God's decree being carried out.

verses.translation_literal: He sent before them a man; for a slave Joseph was sold.
verses.translation_dramatic: But he had already sent someone ahead of them. A single man, walking out in front, a man sold as a slave. His name was Joseph.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalmist now changes the angle: while the famine was being called, a man was already on the road ahead. The sentence has a hinge. 'He sent a man' is God's act, and 'Joseph was sold' is the human crime that carried it out. The two halves sit side by side without a word to explain the paradox, and that is the point: Joseph says the same to his brothers, 'God sent me before you' (Gen 45:5, as Rashi cites). Notice that the name Joseph is held back until the very last word, so the audience hears 'a man', then 'a slave', then the name. Play the delay as a reveal. The KJV 'who was sold for a servant' blurs 'ʿeved' as a polite 'servant'; the Hebrew is a slave, a bought person, and a purchase price was paid (Gen 37:28: twenty shekels of silver, the price of a young man). The BBE 'given as a servant for a price' adds 'for a price', which the verse does not state.

philological_notes.note: 'As a slave', with lamed of the predicate: he was sold to become a slave. Radak: 'for the sake of a slave', i.e. to be a slave. The word is slave, not 'servant' as in the KJV.
'Sent'; Rashi, Meiri and Malbim tie the verb to Joseph's own words in Genesis 45:5, 7: God sent me before you.

verses.translation_literal: They afflicted his foot with the shackle; his soul came [into] iron.
verses.translation_dramatic: They bound his foot in the shackle and bent it down in pain. And the iron was not only on the body: his very self was drawn into it, down to the person he was.
verses.directors_commentary: The camera comes in close on a single foot. The Hebrew is blunt: 'they afflicted'. The verb is ʿinnu, the same verb as the afflictions of Egypt and of Hagar, so the imprisonment is already cast as the first stage of Israel's own future suffering. The written text (Ketiv) has 'feet' and the reading (Qere) the singular 'foot'; the shackle (kevel) was a metal fetter for the ankles, a standard slave restraint. The KJV 'he was laid in iron' flattens the second line. Literally it is 'his soul came [into] iron': the verb בָּאָה is feminine and agrees with the feminine nefesh, so the soul is the one that comes, and Ibn Ezra says a bet is missing, 'into iron'. The familiar English 'iron entered his soul' makes the iron the subject; that is the reading of the Targum and the Vulgate, and it is the source of the English idiom, but it is not what the Hebrew agreement gives. Nefesh is 'soul, life, self, throat'; the STEPBible gloss 'neck' and the BBE 'neck … in iron bands' rely on the sense 'throat', but Meiri and Radak read it as the whole person: the body is chained, and so the self suffers (Radak). Rashi (via the Tanhuma) adds a midrash that an iron collar was placed under his chin. Let the actor feel the weight: the iron is not only on him, he is taken into it. Genesis itself (39:20) says only that he was put in the royal prison, so the shackles come from the psalm and are the psalmist's own knowledge.

philological_notes.note: 'His soul came [into] iron'. The verb is Qal perfect feminine and agrees with the feminine nefesh, so nefesh is the subject, and 'iron' is where it arrives; Ibn Ezra supplies the missing bet ('into iron'), and Metzudat David paraphrases 'his soul came in fetters of iron'. The English 'iron entered his soul' reverses the roles; it is the Targum's and the Vulgate's reading. Nefesh can be 'throat' or 'neck' (so STEPBible and BBE), but Radak and Meiri say that the nefesh stands for the person, who suffers when the body is afflicted.
Piel of 'anah: to humble, afflict, oppress; the verb of the Egyptian oppression (Ex 1:11), here applied to Joseph. Ibn Ezra notes that the subject is left unnamed.

verses.translation_literal: Until the time his word came, the saying of YHWH refined him.
verses.translation_dramatic: So it stayed, until the hour when what he had said came true. Until then the word of the LORD held him in the fire and tested him, as a smith tests silver.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse has two pivots. First, 'his word': whose? The Hebrew does not say, and the commentators split. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David read it as Joseph's: the interpretation of the dreams that finally came true. Rashi and Malbim read it as God's own word, his decree about Israel's descent to Egypt. Both are possible; play the ambiguity and do not settle it. Second, 'refined' (tzeraftehu): צָרַף is a smelter's word, to melt metal and burn off the dross (Ps 12:7; 66:10). The KJV's 'tried him' is correct but pale; it drops the furnace. The scene is a goldsmith's, with the prison as the crucible, which is why Rashi finds in it Joseph's test with Potiphar's wife and his time in prison. 'The saying of YHWH' (imrat YHWH) is the poetic word for God's promise; the same phrase is used of pure, refined speech in Psalm 12:7, so the verse implies that the word itself is what has been refined, and the one who suffered under it is tested by it.

philological_notes.note: To smelt, refine; of testing a person as metal is tested. The subject is the feminine 'saying' (imrah), the object suffix 'him'. Meiri and Radak read the metal image as Joseph's words being found true and pure before Pharaoh, as silver from the fire.
'His word', Joseph's or God's. Ibn Ezra reads Joseph's interpretation; Rashi and Malbim read God's decree.

verses.translation_literal: A king sent and untied him, a ruler of peoples, and he opened [the way for] him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then a king sent for him. The ruler over many nations sent, and the knots of the prisoner's chains were undone, and every door was opened to him.
verses.directors_commentary: The reversal is built in two beats of the same event, an A–B–A–B shape: 'a king sent and loosed him' and 'a ruler of peoples and opened him'. The second line is not another act but a bigger title for the same man: Pharaoh, now called ruler of peoples. It is the largest possible reversal for a slave in irons, and the Hebrew puts the king, 'melekh', right after the verb, so the audience hears the power before the pardon. STEPBible gives both verbs the same gloss, but they differ: the first, וַיַּתִּירֵהוּ, is 'untied, loosed' (the root is the one for undoing a knot or letting someone go); the second, וַיְפַתְּחֵהוּ, is 'opened', as one opens a lock or a door (Metzudat Zion cites Job 12:18, where God 'opens' the bonds of kings). The KJV 'let him go free' for the second verb is a paraphrase that hides the repetition of images. The BBE's 'sent men to take off his chains' adds the men. In the ancient Near East a prisoner of the crown could only be released by the crown, which is why Malbim notes that only a ruler of peoples had the power to remove the penalty that had been laid on him.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of natar: to release, loosen, untie. It is the root of the verb 'untie' as for knots or fetters; the STEPBible gloss 'set free him' blurs the contrast with the next verb.
Piel of patach, 'open': he opened (the bonds, the prison) for him. Metzudat Zion compares Job 12:18, 'he opens the discipline of kings'.

token_glosses.gloss: and he opened [the way for] him

verses.translation_literal: He set him master of his house, and ruler over all his possession.
verses.translation_dramatic: He made him lord of his own house, and gave him rule over everything he owned.
verses.directors_commentary: Joseph was a slave in verse 17, and the vocabulary now answers it, word for word. He was an 'eved', a slave; he becomes an 'adon', a master (Ibn Ezra notices the pairing). The household in question is the royal court: the title in Genesis 41:40 is 'over my house', which in Egyptian practice is the steward of the palace, the head of the whole administration. 'Possession' (qinyan) is anything acquired: livestock, land, stores. The KJV's 'substance' is old English for 'property', and 'lord' is fine for adon, but a modern actor should hear 'master' as a man who is now obeyed by those who sold and chained him. Malbim reads the verse as the first of three steps Pharaoh gives him, from house to land to counsellors, which carry over into the next verse. The text states only the title; it does not describe how Joseph used it.

philological_notes.note: 'Master, lord': the opposite of 'eved' in verse 17. Ibn Ezra points out that the word is chosen to answer 'was sold as a slave'.
'His acquisition, his property' (from qanah, to acquire/buy). KJV 'substance' is an archaic word for wealth.

verses.translation_literal: To bind his officials at his soul, and his elders he makes wise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even the king's own officials were bound by his word, as he saw fit; and the elders of the court sat at his feet and learned wisdom.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse describes the extent of the power, and it is startling: he can bind (have imprisoned or restrain) Pharaoh's own officials, and the old men of the court become his pupils. The key is the little phrase 'in his nefesh', literally 'at his soul', meaning 'as he wishes, as his own self desires'. The KJV 'at his pleasure' is right and reads smoothly; Metzudat Zion's parallel is Psalm 27:12, 'do not give me up to the nefesh (will) of my foes'. Rashi reads it differently, as affection, 'they were bound to him in love' (1 Sam 18:1), and Meiri offers a third reading, 'to avenge himself'. The Hebrew allows all three, so the line is an ironic echo: the man who was bound (asur) now has the right to bind (le'esor), with the same root. Hold that echo: the prisoner has become the one who imprisons. 'Elders' (zeqenim) are not necessarily old; Radak explains that the word means those expected to have wisdom, i.e. the counsellors. The KJV's 'senators' is a Roman anachronism, and the BBE's 'law-givers' translates the translators' guess, not the word. 'Makes wise' (yechakkem) is a Piel, 'teaches wisdom'; the pupils are the king's own advisers.

philological_notes.note: 'To bind'. The root is the same as the noun for prisoner (asir) and for Joseph's own bondage, so the verse reverses his condition: the bound one now binds. Radak: it gave him power to imprison the great men of Pharaoh, as Pharaoh could.
'At his soul, at his will': nefesh as desire (Ps 27:12). Radak and Metzudat David: 'by his will'. Rashi reads it as affection (1 Sam 18:1).
Piel: 'to make wise, to teach'. Ibn Ezra compares Job 35:11, 'he teaches us more than the beasts of the earth'. Metzudat David: he taught wisdom to Pharaoh's elders.

verses.translation_literal: And Israel came [to] Egypt, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then Israel came down to Egypt. Jacob, an old man, lived as a stranger in the land of Ham.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now reaches the point it has been steering toward: the whole family arrives. Joseph's rise has led here, and the text says it with a poetic double: the same person in two lines, first as Israel, then as Jacob, and the same place in two names, first as Egypt (Mitzrayim), then as the 'land of Ham'. The doubling is not padding; Malbim reads the name change as a drop in rank, from Israel the prince to Jacob the guest, which would explain why the second line says 'sojourned' (gar), the word for a resident alien without land rights. The verb tells you what to play: this is not a conquest or a settlement but life on someone else's sufferance. 'Land of Ham' is a poetic name for Egypt, as Mizraim was Ham's son (Gen 10:6). The exact phrase occurs three times, here, in 105:27 and in 106:22; Ps 78:51 has the related 'tents of Ham'. The KJV leaves 'Ham' untouched, so the reader hears a personal name without being told it is Egypt. In this psalm, verse 27 will look back to the same geography as the setting of the plagues.

philological_notes.note: A poetic name for Egypt, after Ham, the father of Mizraim (Gen 10:6). The exact phrase is found in Ps 105:23, 105:27 and 106:22; Ps 78:51 says 'tents of Ham'. Radak and Meiri say it is Egypt; Radak adds that the descent in the time of famine fulfilled the decree 'between the pieces' (Gen 15:13).

'Sojourned, lived as a resident alien': the status of a stranger without land. It is the same verb as the patriarchs' life in Canaan (Gen 12:10; 26:3), so Jacob's whole life is framed as being a guest.

verses.translation_literal: And he made his people very fruitful, and made it mighty from its foes.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there the LORD made his people fruitful, so fruitful, and made them stronger than the ones who would soon be their enemies.
verses.directors_commentary: The window closes on growth, and the verbs are the ones of Genesis: 'be fruitful' (pru) is God's first blessing to humankind (Gen 1:28), and here the Hiphil 'made fruitful' (vayyefer) says that God did it, and the Egyptians did not intend it. 'Very' (me'od) hammers the point. The second verb is a pun on the same family of sounds: 'made mighty' (vayya'atzimehu), the root of 'ʿatzum', the word Pharaoh uses of Israel in Exodus 1:9 ('the people of Israel are more numerous and mighty (ʿatzum) than we'). The KJV 'stronger than their enemies' is right in sense but the Hebrew has min-tzarav, 'from his foes', a comparative, where 'foes' (tzarim) are in the future for the verse: Meiri and Radak remark that the Egyptians are called foes by their later role, since at that moment they were hosts. Malbim connects this directly to Exodus 1: growth is what turned host to enemy. Notice the grammar: 'his people' is masculine singular, and the verb takes a masculine singular suffix, 'made him mighty', so the people is one body. The KJV's 'them' hides this unity.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of parah, 'to be fruitful': causative, 'he made fruitful'. Echoes Gen 1:28 and Ex 1:7 ('the children of Israel were fruitful'). Rashi: the Holy One made them fruitful and many.
'More than his foes', a comparative min. Radak, Meiri: the Egyptians, who are called foes by what they later became. Malbim ties it to Exodus 1:9–10.

verses.translation_literal: He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal craftily with his servants.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then the welcome wore thin. The same hearts that had opened to the strangers turned, slowly, like a key in a lock, and what had been fear became hatred of his people, and hatred became cunning, schemes whispered against the ones who served him.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm: the gift of growth in verse 24 is followed at once by the backlash. Egypt's hatred is not left to politics alone. The verb הפך is the same one that will turn water to blood in verse 29, so the heart-turn and the plague-turn are the same divine act in two registers. Play it as a shift in the room's temperature, not an explosion.

The KJV 'deal subtilly' is archaic, and today 'subtle' sounds like finesse. The Hebrew להתנכל is a reflexive form of a root for scheming and treachery, and its other great use is Gen 37:18, where the brothers 'conspired' against Joseph. Metzudat Zion cites exactly that verse. The Hebrew also says 'servants' (עבדיו), the same word used for Moses next verse, so Israel as a whole is cast as God's household, not just a foreign minority. Meiri links it to Pharaoh's 'let us deal wisely' (Exod 1:10).

philological_notes.note: A reflexive verb for plotting craftily or treacherously. It names the conspiracy of Joseph's brothers in Gen 37:18, which is why the psalm's own Joseph story, a few verses earlier, echoes here.
God is the subject in the active reading: he 'turned' their heart. Radak allows the passive 'their heart turned'. The same verb opens verse 29, so the heart and the Nile are turned alike.

verses.translation_literal: He sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he had chosen in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he sent someone. Moses, his servant, and beside him Aaron, the one he had chosen. Two men walked out toward the throne of the strongest king on earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb שלח, 'send', runs through this part of the psalm: Joseph is sent ahead (v. 17), the king sends to free him (v. 20), God sends Moses here, and in verse 28 he sends darkness. Moses and darkness share the verb, so both are instruments. Moses is 'his servant', the title the psalm has used of Abraham in verse 6 and of Abraham again in verse 42. Aaron is the one 'chosen'; Malbim says Moses is sent as a servant and Aaron as the chosen priest, since only Aaron's line was chosen for the priesthood.

The KJV 'and Aaron whom he had chosen' inserts an 'and' that the Hebrew lacks, which makes Aaron a second item in a list. The Hebrew sets Aaron in apposition to Moses, with the odd final בו, 'chosen in him', which English drops. Ibn Ezra and Meiri note that Aaron was Moses's mouthpiece, which explains why the signs in the next verse are done by a plural subject.

philological_notes.note: 'Whom he chose in him': the verb takes the preposition ב, which English renders as 'chosen' only. In Malbim's reading the choice refers to the priesthood.

verses.translation_literal: They set among them the words of his signs, and wonders, in the land of Ham.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they set them down among the Egyptians, one by one: the words that were signs, the signs that were wonders, planted in the soil of Ham like seeds no one had asked for.
verses.directors_commentary:
The structure is unusual: 'the words of his signs', where Exodus has simply 'signs and wonders'. The psalmist makes the message part of the event: each plague is a spoken word first. Malbim distinguishes the signs, which came with a warning, from the wonders, which came as punishment without warning (lice, boils, darkness), a distinction he draws from Psalm 78.

The KJV 'shewed' softens the verb שׂים, 'set, place', which is deliberate, as if the signs were placed like objects. 'Ham' is a poetic name for Egypt (the Hebrew Mizraim is Ham's son in Gen 10:6), and it sets the narrative in the old world of the nations before Israel.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'the words of his signs'. It may mean 'the matters (acts) of his signs', as YLT's 'the matters'; the double sense of דבר as word and thing is kept alive by the surrounding 'word' of verse 28.
Ham, ancestor of Egypt in the table of nations (Gen 10:6), used in the Psalms as a poetic name for Egypt.

verses.translation_literal: He sent darkness and made it dark, and they did not rebel against his word.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sent darkness, and the darkness came: a dark so thick it had weight. And nothing rebelled. Not the light, not the dark, not the ones who carried his word. It was said, and it was so.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens its plague list with darkness, the ninth in Exodus, out of order. Ibn Ezra reasons that darkness is the plague after which Pharaoh first allowed Israel to leave and worship, so it comes first; Malbim says it marks the end of the first nine, the signs and wonders. Either way, the psalmist is not reciting a table but remembering what mattered. Radak says it is not a complete list on purpose, since the Torah already has one.

The Hebrew repeats the root חשך twice: 'he sent dark and darkened', a figura etymologica that the KJV preserves, which is right. The oddity is the last phrase: 'they did not rebel against his word'. Who? Rashi, Metzudat David and Meiri read it of the plagues themselves, which obeyed. Others read it of Moses and Aaron, who did not disobey, as Radak also allows. The word is written in the singular (דברו) and read in the plural (דבריו); Radak says the sense is the same, one general and one particular. The KJV 'rebelled not' is archaic but accurate.

philological_notes.note: A causative (hiphil) of the same root as 'darkness': he made it dark. The paronomasia is lost in no English version if 'dark' is repeated.
To rebel or be defiant. Rashi and Metzudat David take the plagues as subject: they did not change his word.

verses.translation_literal: He turned their waters into blood, and caused their fish to die.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the river turned. Every water in the land of Egypt, the channel, the pool, the jar by the door, went red and thick, and under the red the fish went still.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb הפך returns from verse 25: the heart was turned, and now the water is turned. The Nile was Egypt's life, its god-given highway and its irrigation, and in the religious world of Egypt the river was divine, so this is a polemic as well as a disaster. The text says only 'their waters', which includes all water, not just the river.

The KJV 'slew their fish' is fair, though the Hebrew is the causative of 'die': he made their fish die, and the cause is the blood. Meiri observes that fish can live only in water, which is why this plague kills them. Note Ibn Ezra's remark that the psalm leaves out the plague of the Nile monsters (תנינים), which was not a plague.

philological_notes.note: Collective noun 'fish', singular in form (feminine singular with the suffix), so 'their fish' is a whole population, not individual fish.

verses.translation_literal: Their land swarmed frogs, in the rooms of their kings.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the land swarmed. Frogs in the fields, frogs in the streets, frogs, past every guard and every door, in the very rooms where their kings slept.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb שרץ is used in Genesis of the teeming of creatures in the waters (Gen 1:20), so here the creation is reversed: the land teems with what belongs in the water. The KJV 'brought forth frogs in abundance' makes the land a mother; the Hebrew has the land as the subject of a transitive verb, 'swarmed frogs', which is rough and strange, as though the land itself produced them. Ibn Ezra explains the unusual masculine verb with the land (ארץ), and Radak adds that the frogs came from the Nile, but the land is named because they filled every pool in it.

The point of 'the rooms of their kings' is that even the court, the most protected space, is invaded. Meiri quotes Exod 7:28, the frogs coming 'into your house and your bedroom and onto your bed'. The plural 'kings' may be a plural of majesty or may refer to the chain of Pharaohs; the KJV keeps the plural, and so do I. BBE changes it to the singular.

philological_notes.note: To swarm, teem. A masculine verb with feminine 'land'; Ibn Ezra notes that ארץ is sometimes masculine. Metzudat Zion: the word means producing offspring in great numbers.
Inner rooms, bedchambers; the most private parts of a house or palace.

verses.translation_literal: He spoke, and there came a swarm, gnats, in all their territory.
verses.translation_dramatic: He spoke, and it came: a swarm, a cloud that hummed and bit, and gnats like dust given wings, over every border of the land.
verses.directors_commentary:
'He spoke, and it came' recurs in verse 34 and is the psalm's refrain of divine power: the word precedes the event. The two plagues named here are the fourth and third, in reverse order. Ibn Ezra says the swarm is mentioned first since it was harsher. Malbim says the gnats had never left Pharaoh when the swarm came, so the two plagues were together.

The word ערב is a swarm, probably of flies, though the Hebrew does not name the creature, and Jewish tradition is split (Radak reads it as wild beasts, 'the evil beasts'). KJV 'divers sorts of flies' guesses, YLT 'beetle' guesses another way, and BBE 'dog-fly' a third. כנים is traditionally 'lice' (KJV, ASV) and is sometimes 'gnats' or 'mosquitoes'. The Hebrew 'in all their territory' is the same word גבול used of the trees in verse 33, a border the creatures ignore.

philological_notes.note: A swarm, from a root for mixing. The creature is unnamed in Hebrew; the traditional 'flies' is an interpretation, and Radak takes it as wild beasts.
Lice or gnats. The identification is uncertain; the KJV 'lice' is traditional, 'gnats' also.

verses.translation_literal: He gave their rains hail, a fire of flames [was] in their land.
verses.translation_dramatic: He gave them hail where the rain should be, hard white stones out of a sky that had always given water, and with the hail, fire, a flame running over the ground.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew is as compact as a sentence can be: 'he gave their rains hail'. The rain, normally a blessing, becomes the weapon, and in Egypt, where rain is rare and the Nile does the work, hail is unnatural. The second half 'fire of flames' echoes Exod 9:23-24, where fire flashed among the hail.

The KJV 'gave them hail for rain' is good in sense, but 'flaming fire' flattens the construct 'fire of flames', which Radak says can be turned around either way. Malbim notes that the psalm skips the plagues of pestilence and boils, because Pharaoh never asked Moses to remove them; Ibn Ezra says the same of the boils. This is a scholar's explanation for why the list is not complete.

philological_notes.note: Plural 'rains', that is, rainstorms. The hail takes the place of the rain.

verses.translation_literal: And he struck their vine and their fig tree, and broke the trees of their territory.
verses.translation_dramatic: The hail came down on the vineyards and the fig trees, the shade and the sweetness of the land, and split the trees along every boundary, until the orchards stood bare.
verses.directors_commentary:
The vine and the fig are the markers of settled prosperity: in the Bible they stand for peace and plenty ('every man under his vine and under his fig tree'). Ibn Ezra says they are named as the most valued of the tree-fruits, which a person can live on even without bread. Radak says they were the main trees of Egypt.

The KJV 'smote their vines also' adds 'also', which is not in the Hebrew. The verb ויך 'struck' is used of the firstborn in verse 36, so the blow that falls on the trees falls later on the children: the psalm uses one verb for both. 'Broke' (שבר) is the same verb used of breaking a bone, which is why 'brake' feels right for wood.

philological_notes.note: To strike. The same verb, in the same form, starts verse 36, tying the orchard to the firstborn.

verses.translation_literal: He spoke, and there came locust and young locust, and there was no number.
verses.translation_dramatic: He spoke, and they came: locust and locust and locust, a moving wall of wings, and no one counting could ever have reached the end.
verses.directors_commentary:
'He spoke, and it came' again, as in verse 31: the plague is not a natural event but an answer to a word. The two Hebrew locust words are אַרְבֶּה, the common one, and יֶלֶק, which is either a stage of the insect or a kind. Radak and Meiri say yelek is a kind of locust; Malbim says arbeh ate the plants and yelek the fruit.

The KJV 'caterpillers' is wrong: ילק is not a caterpillar, though the English word was close to 'larva'. The ending 'without number' (אין מספר) is the psalm's way of saying what Exodus says as 'such as had never been'. The numberless swarm is also a bitter reversal of verse 24, in which God made his people numerous: now the number belongs to the locusts.

philological_notes.note: A kind or stage of locust. Radak and Meiri say it is a kind of arbeh; KJV 'caterpiller' is a guess that misleads.

verses.translation_literal: And it ate all vegetation in their land, and it ate the fruit of their ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: And it ate. Every green blade in their land, it ate. And then the fruit of the ground itself, it ate that too, until the fields were bare as a threshing floor.
verses.directors_commentary:
The repeated verb ויאכל ('and it ate', twice) is the sound of the locusts: a grinding chew that does not stop. Say it twice, slowly. The first meal is vegetation (עשב), the second is the fruit of the ground (פרי אדמתם). Ibn Ezra and Radak say the fruit is what the hail had left over, which fits the sequence of verses 32-33.

The KJV varies the verb: 'did eat up' and 'devoured'. The Hebrew uses the same verb both times, and the repetition is the point, as in YLT. The 'ground' in the second clause (אדמה) is the arable soil, not 'land' (ארץ) as in the first.

philological_notes.note: Green plants, herbage, as opposed to trees; the food of animals and of the land's first growth.

verses.translation_literal: And he struck every firstborn in their land, the beginning of all their vigor.
verses.translation_dramatic: And last, the night. He struck every firstborn in the land: the first of every house, the first sign of strength each family had, the beginning of all their vigor, gone in one silence.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tenth plague, and the first death of people in the psalm. The Hebrew says 'every firstborn' (כל בכור), and the second half, 'the beginning of all their vigor', repeats the thought in new words: Radak says the verse doubles itself, and Metzudat David adds that it is the first of the strength that came from them. In the ancient world the firstborn son was the heir, the carrier of the name and the labour force, so this is a blow to the future.

The KJV 'the chief of all their strength' reads ראשית as 'chief'; it is the beginning, the first-fruits of vigor, the same phrase as 'the beginning of my strength' in Jacob's blessing of Reuben (Gen 49:3), as Meiri notes. The Hebrew אוֹן is a bodily word of vigor, with a procreative hint. Malbim says the firstborn were struck only in Egypt, but 'the beginning of their vigor' was struck wherever Egyptians lived. Ibn Ezra stresses that the firstborn of Israel were spared.

philological_notes.note: 'The beginning of their vigor': the phrase comes from Gen 49:3 (ראשית אוני), as Meiri notes. און can mean strength or procreative power. Metzudat Zion connects it to Isa 40 ('abundance of might').

verses.translation_literal: And he brought them out with silver and gold, and there was none stumbling among his tribes.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then he led them out, and they went laden: silver on their shoulders, gold in their hands. Twelve tribes walked out of the dark, and not one of them faltered, not one fell behind.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalm now leaves the plagues behind and tells only the Exodus itself. Play the silver and gold as plunder that was never taken but given: Exodus 12:35-36 says the Egyptians handed over their valuables when asked, a point the commentators (Meiri on Ps 105:37) tie back to God's word to Abraham about leaving 'with great substance'. For slaves, who owned nothing, this is the reversal of the whole story. In antiquity, precious metal was portable wealth, the only kind a people on foot could carry.

The KJV adds 'also', which is not in the Hebrew, and renders כושל as 'feeble person'. The Hebrew is a participle, 'one stumbling', a word about the legs. A people of hundreds of thousands, in a desert, with no stumbler: that is the claim, and it is a claim of miraculous health, not just of wealth. Ibn Ezra and Meiri hear 'poor' in it; Radak 'poor and weak'. Either way, the line says that no tribe was left behind. Note 'his tribes': the singular 'his' still belongs to God's people, which the KJV 'their' smooths over.

philological_notes.note: A participle, 'one who stumbles'. The root covers physical stumbling and failure of strength and, by extension, poverty. The KJV 'feeble person' flattens the image of a body that trips.
'Among his tribes': the singular suffix treats the people as one body, with 'his' referring back to the collective Israel; the KJV 'their tribes' makes it plural.

verses.translation_literal: Egypt was glad at their going out, for their dread had fallen upon them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Egypt was glad to see them go. Glad! The very land that had held them tight let out its breath, for the dread of them had come down on the Egyptians like a weight, and they wanted only to be rid of them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the most surprising line in the stretch: the oppressor rejoices. After the tenth plague the Egyptians urged Israel to leave, 'for we are all dying' (Ex 12:33), and Ibn Ezra and Meiri read the gladness through that fear. So play the Egyptians not as gloating but as relieved, even grateful, the way a house relaxes when the sick person is carried out.

The last phrase is built on a double 'them'. 'Their dread had fallen upon them' means the dread that Israel inspired fell on Egypt, as Metzudat David says. The KJV 'the fear of them fell upon them' keeps the ambiguity, and the ASV adds a past perfect, 'had fallen', which is right: the fear came first, the gladness after. 'Fell' is the same verb (נפל) the Hebrew uses for a body dropping, which gives the dread a physical weight, as if it landed on the Egyptians' shoulders.

philological_notes.note: 'Dread of them', with the pronoun as the object of dread: the fear Israel caused, not the fear Israel felt. The same root names terror felt before a powerful god or person.

verses.translation_literal: He spread out a cloud for a covering, and fire to give light [by] night.
verses.translation_dramatic: He unfurled a cloud above them like a tent drawn wide against the sun, and when the day went down, he lit a fire in the dark so that the night would not close in on them.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the desert the enemy is the sun. A cloud by day is shade, and a fire by night is light and warmth when the temperature drops sharply. Sound the picture as a household one: a tent flap and a lamp. The Hebrew verb פרשׂ is used of spreading a net, a cloth, a tent, and that is the image.

The KJV 'covering' is fine, but it hides a debate the commentators have over מסך. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it can mean a curtain in front, as with the 'screen' of the Tabernacle door, and that the cloud went ahead of them on the march and spread over them when they halted. Meiri adds that the cloud was long enough to do both. Malbim, following the Rabbis, has it over their heads and around them as well. Because the Hebrew does not say 'over them', do not stage it as a roof only.

philological_notes.note: A screen or covering; the same noun names the curtain at the Tabernacle entrance (Ex 27:16). Whether it is a canopy above or a curtain ahead is exactly what the commentators dispute.

verses.translation_literal: [Israel] asked, and he brought quail, and the bread of heaven he satisfied them.
verses.translation_dramatic: They asked. And he brought them quail out of the evening sky, and then, with the dew rising, bread from heaven itself, until they had had enough.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hunger scene, in a single breath. The Hebrew gives the verb 'asked' no subject; the commentators supply Israel, who asked for meat in the Wilderness of Sin (Ex 16, as Meiri cites), and the KJV supplies 'the people'. Play the request as a complaint the LORD answers anyway: the Psalm omits the grumbling and tells only the answering, which is the Psalm's whole method.

The word שׂלו is quail, small migratory birds that cross the Sinai in exhausted flocks in spring and can be caught by hand, which is why the verb is 'brought', not 'made'. 'Bread of heaven' is manna (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David). A modern reader pictures a loaf; the Hebrew 'bread' is 'food' in general. The KJV 'bread of heaven' is literal, and the BBE's 'birds' loses the specific word. Note the closing verb: ישׂביעם, 'he satisfied them', the root of the word 'full', so the line ends not on the miracle but on the people being full.

philological_notes.note: Quail, the migratory bird; Metzudat Zion calls it 'a fat bird'. The Hebrew is a collective noun.
'Bread of heaven', identified by the commentators with manna. The unaltered Hebrew 'bread' is the general word for food.

verses.translation_literal: He opened a rock, and waters flowed; they went in the dry places [as] a river.
verses.translation_dramatic: He opened the rock. And the water came, first a trickle, then a rush, and it ran through the parched ground as a river runs, where nothing had run before.
verses.directors_commentary:
Water is the single thing a desert people cannot do without, and a rock is the last place anyone looks for it. 'Opened' is the verb used for a gate or a mouth, so the rock is a door the LORD unlocks. The commentators place this at Rephidim (Radak, Malbim).

The KJV 'gushed out' is a little too dramatic for the verb זוב, which means 'to flow, to run', and Metzudat Zion defines it as 'to drip'; Malbim says the water began drop by drop and then grew to a stream. Do not play a burst. The Hebrew 'dry places' is plural, a whole country of dry places, which the KJV keeps. The last word, 'river', has no 'like' in it; the Hebrew simply sets 'river' beside 'dry places', and the contrast does the work.

philological_notes.note: A plural of ציה, parched, waterless ground; it is the exact opposite of what 'river' names. Ibn Ezra comments on the plural form.
'Flowed, ran'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as dripping, which softens the KJV 'gushed out'.

verses.translation_literal: For he remembered the word of his holiness, [and] Abraham his servant.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD remembered. He had given his holy word long ago to Abraham, his servant, and across the years of slavery and the miles of desert, he had not let it go.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the Psalm gives the reason for everything it has just narrated: God 'remembered', which in Hebrew is never a mental event but a decision to act. The audience knew the promise from Genesis 15; Rashi on Ps 105:42 quotes both halves, 'afterward they shall come out with great substance' and 'in the fourth generation they shall return here', and so the silver and gold of verse 37 are the fulfilment of a word spoken to a man who was dead centuries before.

The KJV 'his holy promise' makes it a legal pledge. The Hebrew is 'the word of his holiness': a word set apart, belonging to the sacred sphere, which cannot be revoked. The second 'object marker' before Abraham also leaves the syntax open, and the KJV, 'and Abraham his servant', treats Abraham as a second thing remembered; the YLT's 'with Abraham' reads it as the one the word was made to. Both are possible. 'Servant' is a title of honour here, the sort a king gives a loyal courtier. Radak and Meiri add that the generation of the Exodus did not deserve this and was saved for Abraham's sake.

philological_notes.note: 'To remember' in the Bible means to act on what one holds in mind; here, to fulfil a covenant.
'The word of his holiness': a promise that belongs to the sphere of the sacred. The commentators (Rashi, Metzudat David) identify it with the promise in Genesis 15.

verses.translation_literal: And he brought out his people with joy, with a ringing cry, his chosen ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he led his people out in gladness, with a ringing cry going up from them, his own chosen ones, singing on the road.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalm repeats 'brought out' from verse 37, and the circle closes: the same verb that opened the Exodus now ends it with a sound. ששון is the joy of a feast or a wedding, and רנה is a high, ringing cry, the sound a crowd makes at a victory or a harvest. Radak and Ibn Ezra set it against Egypt, which was mourning its firstborn; the two nations leave the same night with opposite voices.

The KJV 'gladness' for רנה loses the sound. 'A ringing cry' is audible, and it is the word's meaning; the ASV 'with singing' is closer. 'Chosen ones' (בחיריו) is a plural, 'his chosen', the same word the Psalm used in verse 6 ('children of Jacob, his chosen ones'), so the audience hears the opening of the Psalm again. Malbim reads it as 'the righteous' who sang songs of praise.

philological_notes.note: A ringing, shrill cry of joy; the Hebrew names a sound, not a feeling, which the KJV 'gladness' loses.
'His chosen ones', plural; Radak says they are chosen 'for their fathers' sake'.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave to them the lands of nations, and the toil of peoples they took possession of.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he gave them the lands of other nations: fields that others had ploughed, houses that others had raised. What peoples had toiled for, they took as their own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone changes from journey to arrival. 'Lands of nations' is plural: not one country but the territories of several peoples. In the ancient Near East land was wealth and identity; to give the land of others is to say that the LORD is the true owner of every border.

The KJV 'the heathen' for גוים is archaic and carries a judgement the Hebrew word does not; it simply means 'nations'. 'The labour of the people' is a literal rendering of עמל, and it is right, but readers take 'labour' as work rather than what the work produced. Metzudat Zion says עמל names a person's wealth, 'because it comes with much toil'; Ibn Ezra lists houses, olive groves and vineyards. So the line means that Israel inherited the finished product of someone else's hard work. Notice 'they took possession', the verb ירש, which is also the word for inheritance, not conquest: the language is of a legacy, not of a siege.

philological_notes.note: 'Toil', and by extension what toil produces: wealth, property, a settled land.
'They took possession of, inherited'; the language of legacy, not only of conquest.

verses.translation_literal: In order that they might keep his statutes, and his instructions they might observe. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: And the purpose of it all was this: that they might keep his statutes, and guard his teachings with care. Praise the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalm ends on a purpose clause, and it turns the whole history into an obligation. Everything from Abraham to the land was given so that Israel would live by God's decrees; Radak and Meiri read the gifts as conditional, and Malbim calls this verse the introduction to the next Psalm, which tells how they did not keep them. Do not play it as a lecture. It is a quiet, almost sober close after the joy of verse 43.

The verbs are a pair: שׁמר 'keep, guard' and נצר 'observe, watch over', and the Hebrew puts the second verb at the end, after its object, for a closing emphasis. The KJV swaps the two verbs ('observe his statutes, and keep his laws') and so loses the Hebrew order; Hebrew חק is a fixed, engraved decree, תורה is teaching or instruction. 'Laws' for תורות flattens the word into the legal sense, and the same word is the name of the Torah. The last word, הללו־יה, is the plural command 'praise Yah!', which the KJV, like most translations, renders as 'Praise ye the Lord' and so loses the divine name. Here it is a shout to the whole assembly.

philological_notes.note: 'In order that', a purpose conjunction; it frames all the gifts of verses 37-44 as given for the sake of obedience.
A plural imperative, 'praise Yah!', where Yah is the short form of the divine name; this is the origin of 'hallelujah'.
